title: Deterministic fallbacks & microbenchmarks for mixed-precision KV-cache alignment
content:
Purpose and scope:

This document specifies deterministic fallback semantics and a focused microbenchmark suite to validate mixed-precision execution paths (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) when interacting with the serving runtime KV cache and scheduler. The goal is to provide unambiguous rules the runtime uses to decide: (1) when to route a request to a lower/higher precision kernel, (2) how to align KV-cache representations across precision transitions, and (3) what telemetry and microbenchmarks to use to verify latency/cost/quality tradeoffs.

Context and motivation:

We operate multiple quantized kernel implementations with differing memory layout, latency, and quality characteristics. In steady-state these kernels reduce per-token cost, but mixed workloads (varying sequence lengths, multi-turn chat, or heterogeneous model variants) require runtime transitions between kernels. Those transitions must not invalidate the KV cache or introduce non-deterministic outputs across retries/fallbacks. Customers expect stable outputs for identical prompts and predictable latency SLOs.

Definitions and constraints:

- Precision flavors: INT8, FP8 (tensor-fp8 variants), GPTQ (post-training quantized weights, per-channel), AWQ (advanced weight-only quantization).
- Kernel: a compiled operator implementation for a specific precision and hardware path (e.g., int8-fused-mha-nv, fp8-matmul-cuda-kerX).
- KV representation: in-memory format of key/value cache slices. Format may be compressed, dequantized, or left in packed quantized form depending on kernel compatibility.
- Deterministic fallback: a runtime behavior where, on kernel failure or policy-triggered fallback, the sequence of outputs for a request is invariant given identical inputs and kernel availability permutations.

High-level policy principles:

1) Explicit compatibility levels: every kernel advertises a compatibility level string (e.g., compat=v1.int8.kv-packed, compat=v2.fp8.dequantized). The scheduler only attempts intra-request transitions between kernels whose compatibility declares either direct compatibility or a supported conversion path.

2) Immutable-response requirement: if a request has already emitted tokens to the client (streaming), the runtime must not switch KV representation in a way that causes non-repeatable continuation tokens. In practice this implies: either keep using the original kernel for that logical conversation until preconfigured boundary conditions, or perform a safe conversion that is bit-for-bit repeatable.

3) Conversion atomicity and versioning: conversions from packed quantized KV to dequantized float must be atomic and produce a new KV version id. Requests reference a KV-version-uuid; any conversion increments the version. The conversion must be recorded with deterministic metadata so a retried request can reproduce the conversion outcome.

KV-cache alignment rules (detailed):

A) Packed->Packed with same bitwidth: allowed without conversion when kernel ABI layout matches. Checksum verification of KV-slice layout required at handshake.

B) Packed->Packed with different packing (e.g., GPTQ per-channel vs AWQ block-wise): not allowed. The scheduler must either convert to dequantized float or re-generate cache from prefix tokens using the target kernel (prefer dequantize for latency-sensitive paths).

C) Packed->Dequantized float (FP32/FP16): allowed via deterministic dequantization routine. The runtime must record quantization metadata (scales, zero points, block-shape) and a canonical dequant routine (documented and versioned) so dequantization is deterministic across hosts and restarts.

D) Dequantized->Packed: allowed only when canonical quantization routine is available and verified to be within quality tolerances for the request's eval set; otherwise disallowed for production traffic.

E) Streaming boundaries: when a stream is live and the incoming request length exceeds the precomputed prefix budget, the runtime will not convert the resident KV cache mid-response unless conversion latency is within the remaining SLO and the conversion is pre-approved by policy. Default production policy: no mid-stream conversions.

Deterministic fallback decision tree (runtime pseudocode in prose):

- On scheduling, pick preferred kernel K_pref by cost/latency profile.
- If K_pref fails to initialize/oom or kernel ABI fails handshake => record failure telemetry and select fallback kernel from descending preference list.
- Before switching kernel for an in-flight request: check KV compatibility. If incompatible, perform deterministic conversion (if policy allows) or fall back to target kernel with cache rehydration plan.
- If conversion would exceed token-latency budget (remaining SLO), choose a kernel with matching ABI or perform safe blocking: respond with graceful degradation (partial response + retry suggestion) per route policy.

Microbenchmark harness: what to measure and why

Purpose: quantify the latency and quality cost of conversions and fallback paths under realistic tokenization/prefix distributions. Measurements will drive scheduler thresholds and safety limits.

Benchmarks to include (each run summarized by distribution and hardware):

1) Prefix rehydrate vs dequant conversion latency: measure end-to-end time to make KV usable by target kernel for a fixed prefix size distribution (0, 32, 128, 512 tokens). Report median/p95/p99.
2) Conversion determinism checksum pass rate: run conversions across hosts (3 different GPU types, 2 driver versions) and verify checksum equality of dequantized buffers. Report failure rate and divergence pattern.
3) Token continuation latency after conversion vs native run: emit next N tokens (N=1..16) and compare latencies and token-level probability divergence metrics (e.g., KL per token, top-1 match rate).
4) Memory amplification: memory footprint delta when converting packed->dequantized and dequant->packed for the peak prefix sizes.
5) Multi-tenant stress: concurrent conversions under heavy scheduler load to detect head-of-line blocking or GC interference.

Microbenchmark outputs and thresholds (proposed initial thresholds):

- conversion_median_latency(prefix=128) < 12ms on A100-40GB for INT8->FP16 dequant path
- conversion_p99_latency(prefix=512) < 65ms
- token_top1_match_rate after conversion >= 99.2% for AWQ->FP16 dequant path on our evaluation prompts
- checksum_divergence_rate across hosts == 0% for canonical dequant routine (any divergence is a release blocker)

Telemetry and instrumentation requirements:

- telemetry tags for every conversion: from_compat, to_compat, prefix_tokens, conversion_time_ms, kv_bytes_in, kv_bytes_out, kernel_failure_reason.
- record deterministic_version_id for each conversion and include in request traces so replay runs can reproduce conversions.
- attach small deterministic sample of first 8 bytes of dequant buffer (hex) to trace for quick sanity checks (sampling only, PII-safe).

Quality and evaluation guidance:

- Define route-level eval prompt sets (50–200 prompts) that capture common failure modes. Each new conversion routine or kernel ABI change must pass through the eval harness to ensure token-level metrics do not regress beyond configured thresholds.
- For AWQ/GPTQ paths where quantization is lossy, record per-layer calibration stats used during online runtime dequant/quant steps to help debugging.

Scheduler integration and rollout guidance:

- Scheduler must treat conversion time as part of kernel initialization cost for scheduling decisions (affects admission control for latency SLOs).
- Canary rollout rule: enable new conversion routine for 1% of traffic with aggressive telemetry and automatic rollback if conversion_p99 > threshold or token divergence increases by configured delta.

Failure modes and mitigations:

- Non-zero checksum divergences: fail fast, revert conversion routine, mark host as quarantine until binaries and drivers reconciled.
- OOM during conversion: fallback to rehydrate-from-prefix with priority queue; if that also fails, respond with a clear service error and return metrics for operator triage.

Operational checklist before enabling conversions in production:

- Run full microbenchmark suite on each target GPU and OS image; capture baseline and accept thresholds.
- Verify checksum parity across at least 3 host images and docker runtime builds.
- Create route-level eval sets and a canary rollout plan (1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%).
- Ensure traces capture conversion deterministic_version_id and provide replay harness to reproduce conversions offline.

Open questions / decisions for next design iteration:

- Should we support streaming-safe in-place packing transforms (zero-copy) on certain hardware? Pros: lower latency. Cons: increased ABI complexity and determinism risk.
- How aggressive should the scheduler be about proactively converting caches on warm-up when a model variant shows a moderate probability of being needed? (memory vs latency tradeoff).
- Standardize a cross-team canonical dequant routine implementation (C++ runtime + CPU fallback) and include versioned test vectors shipped with runtime artifacts.

Appendix: minimal test vectors to include in repo (text form)

- short_prompt_1: "Translate: Hello world" — test prefix sizes [0, 16, 64]
- chat_turn_5: 5-turn multiuser dialog synthesized from production traces (sanitized) — verify streaming boundary behavior
- long_prefix_512: artificially constructed 512-token prefix with repeating patterns to exercise block packing edges

Summary:

This spec mandates deterministic, versioned conversions between KV representations, concrete microbenchmarks and thresholds to validate latency and quality, and explicit scheduler integration rules so that mixed-precision execution paths behave predictably in production. Next steps: review with SRE and product to finalize thresholds, implement the canonical dequant routine and add microbenchmark CI jobs to the runtime repo.
